diagram.title: How many checks does binary search need?
diagram.caption: Change the number of items in a sorted list. A linear search could need to check every one of them.

blocks.text: There is often more than one algorithm that solves a problem. They might all give the right answer, but one might take a second and another might take an hour. Computer scientists compare algorithms by their **[[efficiency]]**: how much **time** (number of steps) and **memory** they need.
Counting steps

We do not time algorithms with a stopwatch, because a faster computer would give a different answer. Instead we count the **steps**, such as the number of comparisons. We usually look at the **[[worst case]]**: the most steps the algorithm could ever need.

head: Items in sorted list
Linear search (worst case)
Binary search (worst case)
blocks.caption: Doubling the list adds only one extra check to a binary search

blocks.text: Every check in a binary search halves what is left, so doubling the size of the list adds just **one** more check. A linear search on a list twice as long could take **twice** as many checks.

head: Linear search
Binary search
rows: Fast: halves the list each time

blocks.text: Binary search is not always the winner. If the list is not sorted you would have to sort it first, which takes time. For a short list, or one you only search once, a linear search is perfectly sensible.
Two algorithms, one problem
Problem: add up all the whole numbers from 1 to 100. Both algorithms below are correct.

blocks.title: Algorithm A: loop
blocks.code:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 100
    total ← total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total

blocks.title: Worked example: which is more efficient?
blocks.context: Compare algorithms A and B for adding 1 to n.
steps: Algorithm A does **one addition for every number**: 100 additions for n = 100, a million for n = 1,000,000.
Algorithm B does **the same small calculation** whatever n is: 100 × 101 ÷ 2 = 5050.
Both give the correct answer, so compare the steps.
As n gets bigger, A gets slower and slower but B stays the same.
blocks.answer: Algorithm B is more efficient. Algorithm A is easier to understand, but its number of steps grows with n.

blocks.text: Sorting algorithms differ too. **Bubble sort** is easy to understand but slow on big lists, because it keeps passing through the whole list. Faster methods, such as **merge sort**, are used for big jobs like sorting every pupil in Northern Ireland by exam result.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Efficiency is how much time (steps) and memory an algorithm uses.
Compare algorithms by counting steps, often in the worst case.
Binary search needs far fewer checks than linear search on a long sorted list.
The most efficient algorithm is not always best: binary search needs a sorted list.
Bubble sort is simple but slow on large lists.

check.q: What does the efficiency of an algorithm describe?
o: Which language it is written in
How much time and memory it uses
check.why: Efficient algorithms use fewer steps and less memory.

check.q: A sorted list has 1,000 items. What is the most checks a binary search needs?
check.why: Halving 1,000 repeatedly takes at most 10 checks.

check.q: When might a linear search be the better choice?
o: The list is huge and sorted
The list is short or unsorted
When the target is in the middle
check.why: No sorting needed, and on a short list the difference is tiny.

check.q: What is the worst case for a linear search on a list of 50 items?
check.why: The target is last, or missing, so every item is checked.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the **efficiency** of an algorithm.
practice.a: How much time / how many steps it takes (1) and how much memory it uses (1) to solve a problem.

practice.q: A library has 100,000 books sorted by title. Explain why a binary search would be more efficient than a linear search for finding a book.
practice.a: Linear search might have to check every one of the 100,000 titles (1). Binary search halves the number of books left with each check (1), so it needs at most about 17 checks (1).

practice.q: Algorithm A uses a loop to add the numbers 1 to n. Algorithm B uses the formula n × (n + 1) ÷ 2. Which is more efficient for large values of n? Explain your answer.
practice.a: Algorithm B (1). It does the same small number of steps whatever n is, while A needs one addition for every number, so it gets slower as n grows (1).

pages.spec: Find and fix errors in an algorithm using tracing and test data
pages.summary: A bug is an error that stops an algorithm working correctly. Debugging means testing, tracing to find the bug, fixing it and testing again; logic errors are the hardest to spot because the algorithm still runs.

diagram.title: The debugging cycle
diagram.caption: Click each stage. Keep going round until the tests all pass.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Run the algorithm with test data where you already know the correct answer.

items.label: Spot
items.detail: Compare the actual output with the expected output. Different? There is a bug.

items.label: Find
items.detail: Use a trace table to dry run the algorithm line by line and see where the values first go wrong.

items.label: Fix
items.detail: Change the faulty line. Change one thing at a time.

items.label: Retest
items.detail: Run all the tests again, to check the fix worked and has not broken anything else.

blocks.text: Almost no algorithm works perfectly first time. An error in an algorithm or program is called a **[[bug]]**, and finding and fixing bugs is called **[[debugging]]**. Good programmers expect bugs and test carefully to find them.
Two kinds of error

head: Syntax error
Logic error
rows: Breaks the rules (grammar) of the language, e.g. a spelling mistake in a keyword or a missing bracket
Follows the rules but gives the wrong result
No: the program will not run until it is fixed
Yes, but the output is wrong
The editor or translator points to the line
Testing and tracing with a trace table

blocks.text: A **[[syntax error]]** is usually easy to find. A **[[logic error]]** is harder, because nothing tells you it is there. You only notice when the answer is wrong, which is why we test.
Common bugs

head: Bug
Example
Fix
rows: A WHILE loop where count never changes
OUTPUT total before the loop that adds it up
Move the OUTPUT after ENDWHILE or NEXT
blocks.caption: Bugs to look out for

blocks.text: Worked example: fixing a broken average
This algorithm should read in five test marks and output the average. Testing with the marks 6, 8, 10, 7 and 9 (total 40, so the average should be **8**) gives **1.8**. Something is wrong.

blocks.title: Broken algorithm
blocks.code:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
    INPUT mark
    total ← mark
NEXT i
average ← total / 5
OUTPUT average

blocks.title: Worked example: trace, find, fix
blocks.context: Trace the broken algorithm with marks 6, 8, 10, 7, 9.
steps: i = 1: mark = 6, total = **6**.
i = 2: mark = 8, total = **8**. The 6 has gone! The total should be 14.
This is where it first goes wrong: `total ← mark` **replaces** the total instead of adding to it.
Carry on: after i = 5, total = 9, so average = 9 / 5 = 1.8. That matches the wrong output.
Fix: change the line to `total ← total + mark`. Retest: total = 6 + 8 + 10 + 7 + 9 = 40, average = 40 / 5 = **8**. Correct.
blocks.answer: The bug was a logic error on line 4. The fixed line is `total ← total + mark`.

blocks.text: Choosing test data
Good **[[test data]]** checks more than just the obvious. For "pass if the mark is 50 or more" (marks out of 100):

head: Type
Example
Why
rows: Typical values the algorithm should handle easily.
Values right at the edge, where `>` and `>=` bugs show up.
blocks.caption: Normal, boundary and erroneous test data

blocks.text: Work out the **expected** output before you test. If you do not know what the right answer is, you cannot tell whether the algorithm got it wrong.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A bug is an error; debugging is finding and fixing it.
Syntax errors break the language rules and stop it running.
Logic errors run but give the wrong result, so testing and tracing are needed.
Common bugs: wrong comparison, off-by-one, infinite loops, wrong order, variables not updated.
Test with normal, boundary and erroneous data, then retest after every fix.

check.q: An algorithm runs but gives the wrong answer. What type of error is this?
check.why: It follows the rules but the logic is wrong.

check.q: `count ← 1`, then `WHILE count <= 3` with `OUTPUT count` inside and nothing else. What happens?
check.why: count never changes, so it is an infinite loop.

check.q: The rule is "pass if 50 or more". Which pair is boundary test data?
check.why: They sit either side of the edge of the rule.

check.q: `WHILE count < 10` should output 1 to 10 but stops at 9. What kind of bug is this?
check.why: It runs one time too few; `<=` fixes it.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **syntax error** and a **logic error**.
practice.a: Syntax error: breaks the rules/grammar of the language, so the program will not run (1). Logic error: the program runs but produces the wrong result / does not do what was intended (1).

practice.q:
This algorithm should output the numbers 1 to 5, but it never stops. Identify the bug and write the corrected algorithm.

`count ← 1`
`WHILE count <= 5`
`    OUTPUT count`
`ENDWHILE`
practice.a: count is never increased, so count <= 5 is always true / infinite loop (1). Add `count ← count + 1` (1) inside the loop, after `OUTPUT count` and before `ENDWHILE` (1).

practice.q: An algorithm gives a cinema discount to anyone **aged 12 or under**. Give **one** normal, **one** boundary and **one** erroneous test value, and the expected result for each.
practice.a: Normal, e.g. 8: discount / 30: no discount (1). Boundary, e.g. 12: discount or 13: no discount (1). Erroneous, e.g. -4 or "ten": rejected / error message (1).

chapters.title: Cyber Security
chapters.intro: Learn how criminals try to attack computers and accounts, and, more importantly, how to stop them: from spotting phishing and building strong passwords to encryption, firewalls, backups, the law and careers in cyber security.

pages.spec: Explain why data and computer systems are valuable and describe the CIA triad
pages.summary: Cyber security protects computers, networks, accounts and data. Good security keeps data Confidential, keeps it correct (Integrity) and keeps it Available when it is needed: the CIA triad.

diagram.title: Which part of CIA is broken?
diagram.caption: Decide which part of the CIA triad each attack damages, then click to check.
head: What happened
CIA part
Why
rows: A pupil reads the teacher's markbook over their shoulder
Someone saw data they were not allowed to see
Someone changes their own test score from 45% to 95%
The data has been altered, so it can no longer be trusted
Ransomware locks every file on the school server
Staff and pupils cannot get to the data when they need it
A hacker posts the school's pupil addresses online
Private personal data has been exposed
The online homework site is flooded with fake traffic and crashes
The system is down, so nobody can use it
Malware swaps the bank details on a supplier's invoice
Data was secretly changed so money goes to the wrong place

blocks.text: Think about everything stored about you in school: your name, address, date of birth, medical notes, attendance, reports and exam results. Now think about your phone: photos, messages, game accounts and saved passwords. All of this is **data**, and to the wrong person it is worth a lot.
**[[Cyber security]]** is the set of methods, tools and habits used to protect computers, networks, accounts and data from being attacked, damaged or accessed without permission.
Why is data so valuable?

head: Who wants it?
What they might do with it
rows: Sell stolen passwords and personal details, steal money, or use your identity to open accounts.
Lock an organisation's files and demand payment to unlock them.
Use data about what you like to target adverts (legally, if they follow the rules).
Take over a social media or game account to embarrass the owner.
Spy on governments and businesses, or disrupt hospitals, power and transport.
blocks.caption: Why people want your data and systems

blocks.text: Systems are valuable too. If a hospital's computers stop working, operations are cancelled. If a school's network is down, registers, lessons and exams are disrupted. Attacking the **system** can do as much harm as stealing the **data**.
The CIA triad
Security experts describe what they are protecting using three ideas, called the **[[CIA triad]]** (nothing to do with the American spy agency!).

head: Letter
Meaning
School example
rows: Only the right people can **see** the data.
Only your teachers and parents can see your report.
The data is **correct** and has not been changed without permission.
Nobody can secretly change your exam marks.
The data and systems **work** when the right people need them.
The register system works at 9 am every morning.
blocks.caption: The three parts of the CIA triad

blocks.title: Worked example: a stolen teacher password
blocks.context: Someone guesses a teacher's password and logs in to the school's management system. Which parts of the CIA triad are at risk?
steps: They can **see** pupils' private details: confidentiality is broken.
They could **change** marks or attendance: integrity is at risk.
They could **delete** records or lock the account: availability is at risk.
blocks.answer: One weak password can put all three parts of the triad at risk, which is why accounts need strong protection.

blocks.text: Not every threat is a criminal. A spilled drink, a fire, a power cut or simply deleting the wrong folder can also destroy data. Good cyber security plans for accidents as well as attacks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Cyber security protects computers, networks, accounts and data.
Data is valuable to criminals, companies and even other countries.
Confidentiality: only the right people can see it.
Integrity: it is correct and has not been tampered with.
Availability: it works when it is needed.

check.q: What does the **I** in the CIA triad stand for?
check.why: Integrity means the data is correct and has not been changed without permission.

check.q: A hacker reads private emails but changes nothing. Which part of the CIA triad is broken?
check.why: Someone has seen data they should not see.

check.q: The school website is knocked offline for a day. Which part of the triad is affected?
check.why: Availability means systems work when people need them.

check.q: Which of these is the best description of cyber security?
o: Protecting systems, networks, accounts and data from attack or damage
check.why: Cyber security is all about protection.

practice.q: Name the **three** parts of the CIA triad.
practice.a: Confidentiality (1); Integrity (1); Availability (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why a criminal might want to steal personal data from a school.
practice.a: Any two: to sell it (1); to commit identity theft / pretend to be someone (1); to demand a ransom from the school (1); to steal money / use for scams (1).

practice.q: A pupil logs in to the school system and changes their attendance record. Explain which part of the CIA triad has been broken.
practice.a: Integrity (1) because the data has been changed without permission so it is no longer accurate/trustworthy (1).

pages.spec: Describe different types of malware and the harm each one can do
pages.summary: Malware is any software written to cause harm. Viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, spyware and adware differ in how they spread and what damage they do.

diagram.title: Match the malware
diagram.caption: Click a type of malware, then the description that matches it.
pairs: Attaches itself to a file and spreads when that file is opened or shared
Spreads across a network by itself, with no help from a user
Looks like a useful program but hides something harmful inside
Locks or encrypts your files and demands payment
Secretly watches what you do and sends it to someone else
Floods you with pop-up adverts and may track your browsing

blocks.text: **[[Malware]]** is short for **mal**icious soft**ware**: any program written on purpose to cause harm. You met some types of malware in e-safety. Here we look more closely at **how each one spreads** and **what it does**, so you can recognise the signs.
Six types of malware

head: Type
How it spreads
What it does
rows: Attaches to a normal file or program. It needs a **person** to open or share the file.
Copies itself into other files; can delete or corrupt data and slow the computer.
Spreads **on its own** across a network, looking for computers with security holes.
Copies itself very fast, using up bandwidth and slowing whole networks.
Disguised as something you want, like a free game, a cheat or a fake app.
Once installed, it can open a 'back door' that lets an attacker control the computer.
Often arrives through a phishing email attachment or a trojan.
Encrypts (scrambles) your files and demands money, usually in cryptocurrency, to unlock them.
Hidden inside free downloads or installed by a trojan.
Secretly records your activity. A *keylogger* records every key you press, including passwords.
Bundled with free software or browser extensions.
Shows unwanted adverts and pop-ups, and may track the sites you visit.
blocks.caption: Types of malware

head: Virus
Worm
rows: Needs a person to help it spread?
Yes: someone must open or share an infected file
No: it is a standalone program
As fast as people share files
Very fast: thousands of computers in minutes

blocks.title: Worked example: the WannaCry attack (2017)
blocks.context: In May 2017 a piece of ransomware called WannaCry spread around the world. It hit many NHS hospitals and GP surgeries in the UK, and some appointments and operations had to be cancelled.
steps: It behaved like a **worm**: it spread by itself between computers on a network.
It was **ransomware**: it encrypted files and demanded payment to unlock them.
It only worked on computers that had **not installed a security update** that Microsoft had released two months earlier.
Organisations with up-to-date computers and good **backups** recovered much more quickly.
blocks.answer: Malware types can be combined. Keeping software updated and keeping backups are two of the best defences.

blocks.text: Warning signs that a device may be infected

items: The computer suddenly becomes very slow or crashes often.
Lots of pop-ups appear, even when no browser is open.
Your browser home page or search engine changes by itself.
Friends receive messages from your account that you did not send.
Files will not open, or have strange new file extensions, and a ransom note appears.

blocks.text: If you see a ransom message on a school computer, **do not** click anything or try to pay. Stop, unplug nothing yourself, and tell your teacher straight away so the technicians can isolate the machine.
Most malware needs **you** to let it in: by opening an attachment, clicking a link or installing something. Thinking before you click stops most of it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Malware is any software designed to cause harm.
A virus needs a person to spread it; a worm spreads by itself.
A trojan pretends to be something useful.
Ransomware locks your files and demands payment.
Spyware secretly watches you; adware floods you with adverts.

check.q: Which type of malware can spread across a network **without** anyone opening a file?
check.why: A worm is standalone and spreads by itself.

check.q: A free 'Robux generator' app secretly lets someone control your laptop. What type of malware is it?
check.why: It is disguised as something you want: a trojan horse.

check.q: What does ransomware do?
o: Encrypts your files and demands payment
check.why: It holds your files to ransom.

check.q: A keylogger is a type of:
check.why: It secretly records your key presses, so it is spyware.

practice.q: Describe **one** difference between a virus and a worm.
practice.a: A virus attaches itself to another file/program (1) whereas a worm is a standalone program (1). OR A virus needs a person to open/share a file to spread (1) whereas a worm spreads by itself across a network (1).

practice.q: Explain what ransomware is and **one** way an organisation can reduce the damage it causes.
practice.a: Malware that encrypts/locks files (1) and demands a payment to unlock them (1). Keep regular backups so files can be restored without paying / keep software updated / use anti-malware (1).

practice.q: Give **two** signs that a computer might be infected with malware.
practice.a: Any two: runs very slowly / crashes (1); unexpected pop-ups (1); home page changes by itself (1); messages sent from your account that you did not send (1); files will not open / ransom note (1).

pages.spec: Describe social engineering techniques, including phishing, smishing, vishing, pretexting and shoulder surfing
pages.summary: Social engineering tricks people rather than computers. Attackers use fake emails, texts, phone calls, made-up stories and simply looking over your shoulder to get passwords and information.

diagram.title: Anatomy of a phishing email
diagram.caption: Click each part of this fake email to see the warning sign.

rows.label: From: support@micros0ft-security.co
rows.detail: The sender address is wrong: a zero instead of an 'o' and a strange domain. Always check the real address, not just the display name.

rows.label: Subject: URGENT!!! Account suspended
rows.detail: Capitals and panic words are used to rush you so you do not stop and think.

rows.label: Dear Student,
rows.detail: A generic greeting. A real organisation that holds your account would normally use your name.

rows.label: Your account will be deleted in 2 hours
rows.detail: A threat with a short deadline. Real organisations do not give you two hours to save your account.

rows.label: Click here to verfy your pasword
rows.detail: Spelling mistakes and a request for your password. Genuine companies never ask for your password by email.

rows.label: Attachment: Account_Form.zip
rows.detail: An unexpected attachment, especially a .zip or .exe file, could contain malware.

blocks.text: You can buy the best security software in the world, but if someone simply **tells you their password**, the software cannot help. **[[Social engineering]]** means tricking or manipulating people into giving away information or access. It attacks the *human*, often called the weakest link.

Social engineers rely on feelings: **fear** ("your account will be closed"), **urgency** ("act now"), **curiosity** ("see who viewed your profile"), **greed** ("you've won") and **trust** ("this is IT support").
Five techniques to know

head: Technique
How it works
Example
rows: Fake **emails** that pretend to be from a trusted organisation, to get you to click a link, open an attachment or type in your details.
An email 'from Netflix' saying your payment failed, with a link to a fake login page.
Phishing by **SMS text message** (or messaging app).
A text 'from Royal Mail' asking you to pay a small fee to redeliver a parcel.
Phishing by **voice**: a phone call or voicemail.
A caller claiming to be from your bank's fraud team asking for a code sent to your phone.
Inventing a believable **story** (a pretext) to get someone to help.
Someone phones the school office pretending to be a parent who 'forgot' a pupil's login.
Watching someone type a password or PIN, in person or with a camera.
A classmate watches you type your password at the start of a lesson.
blocks.caption: Social engineering techniques

blocks.title: Worked example: the fake technician
blocks.context: During lunch a friendly adult in a high-vis vest walks into the computer room and says to a Year 9 pupil: "I'm from the IT company, I need to check the network. Can you log in for me? Your teacher said it's fine."
steps: **Pretexting:** the person has invented a story to seem trustworthy.
**Authority:** the vest and the mention of the teacher make it feel official.
**Pressure:** it is lunchtime, so there is no teacher to check with.
**The right response:** politely say no, do not log in, and tell a member of staff straight away.
blocks.answer: Real technicians never need *your* password. Anyone asking for it is a warning sign.

blocks.text: To beat shoulder surfing: shield the keyboard or PIN pad with your hand, lock your screen when you walk away (**Windows key + L**), and never type a password while someone is watching.

Phishing messages are getting more convincing. Some are sent to one specific person using details found online (this is called *spear phishing*), and AI tools now help criminals write messages without spelling mistakes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Social engineering tricks people, not computers.
Phishing = email; smishing = SMS text; vishing = voice call.
Pretexting uses a made-up story to win trust.
Shoulder surfing means watching someone type a password or PIN.
Attackers use fear, urgency, curiosity, greed and trust.

check.q: A text message claims to be from a delivery company and asks you to pay a redelivery fee. This is:
check.why: SMS + phishing = smishing.

check.q: What is shoulder surfing?
o: Browsing the web on a tablet
Watching someone type their password or PIN
check.why: It is simply looking over someone's shoulder.

check.q: Someone rings pretending to be a parent and makes up a story to get a pupil's login. This is:
check.why: A pretext is an invented story.

check.q: Why is social engineering often successful?
o: It plays on human feelings like fear and trust
It only works on old computers
check.why: It targets people, who can be rushed or tricked.

practice.q: Explain the difference between **phishing** and **vishing**.
practice.a: Phishing uses fake emails / messages to trick people into giving details (1); vishing uses phone calls / voice messages (1).

practice.q: What is **social engineering**? Give **one** example.
practice.a: Tricking/manipulating people into giving away information or access (1). Any valid example, e.g. phishing email, smishing text, pretexting phone call, shoulder surfing (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways a pupil could protect themselves against shoulder surfing.
practice.a: Any two: cover the keyboard/keypad when typing (1); check nobody is watching before typing (1); lock the screen when leaving the computer (1); use a privacy screen filter (1).

pages.spec: Spot the warning signs of a phishing message and know what to do if you receive one
pages.summary: Phishing messages share common warning signs: wrong sender addresses, urgency, generic greetings, odd links and requests for passwords. If in doubt, don't click: check another way and report it.

diagram.title: I've received a suspicious message
diagram.caption: Follow the steps whenever a message makes you unsure.

nodes.label: Suspicious message arrives
nodes.detail: An email, text, DM or call that asks you to click, pay, log in or share something.

nodes.label: Stop and check the signs
nodes.detail: Sender address, urgency, greeting, spelling, links and attachments.

nodes.label: Is it genuine?
nodes.detail: If anything feels wrong, treat it as suspicious.

nodes.label: Check another way
nodes.detail: Go to the real app or website yourself, or ask the person using a contact you already have.

nodes.label: Report and delete
nodes.detail: Tell a teacher or parent. Forward scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk and scam texts to 7726, then delete.

nodes.label: Clicked by mistake?
nodes.detail: Tell an adult at once, change your password from a safe device and turn on 2FA.

blocks.text: Phishing is the most common way that accounts are stolen and malware gets into organisations. The good news: most phishing messages have **warning signs** if you know where to look.
The warning signs

head: Warning sign
What to look for
rows: The display name says 'PayPal' but the actual address is *paypa1-alerts@mail-secure.xyz*. Look for misspellings and odd endings.
"Act within 24 hours or your account will be deleted!"
"Dear Customer" or "Dear User" instead of your name.
Mistakes, odd wording or strange capital letters (although some scams are now perfectly written).
Hover over (or press and hold) a link to see where it really goes before clicking.
Asking for your password, a security code, or bank details.
"You've won a free PS5!" or "Claim 10,000 free V-Bucks".
Files you were not expecting, especially .zip, .exe or documents asking you to 'enable content'.
blocks.caption: How to spot a phishing message

blocks.title: Worked example: spot the signs
blocks.context: Ciarán gets this text: *"HMRC: You are due a tax refund of £248.50. Claim before midnight tonight at hmrc-refund-uk.com/claim"*. He is 13 and does not pay tax.
steps: **Unexpected:** Ciarán does not pay tax, so a refund makes no sense.
**Too good to be true:** free money.
**Urgency:** 'before midnight tonight'.
**Suspicious link:** the real HMRC website ends in **gov.uk**, not *hmrc-refund-uk.com*.
**Action:** don't click; forward the text to **7726** and delete it.
blocks.answer: Four warning signs: this is a smishing scam designed to steal bank details.

blocks.text: Checking links safely

A link's visible text can say anything. What matters is the **real web address**. In a web address, the most important part is the bit just before the first single forward slash, such as `www.bbc.co.uk` in `https://www.bbc.co.uk/news`. Scammers try tricks like `bbc.co.uk.news-login.com`: here the real website is **news-login.com**, not the BBC.

head: Genuine
Fake
rows: Yes, on a page linked from the message

blocks.text: **Don't use the link in the message.** If you think it might be real, open the app or type the website address yourself and log in from there. If there's a real problem, you will see it.

In the UK you can report scam emails to the National Cyber Security Centre by forwarding them to **report@phishing.gov.uk**, and scam texts by forwarding them to **7726** (it spells SPAM on an old phone keypad).
If you have already clicked a link or typed in a password, **don't hide it out of embarrassment**. Tell an adult immediately. The faster a password is changed, the less damage can be done.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Check the real sender address, not just the display name.
Urgency, threats and 'too good to be true' offers are big red flags.
Hover over links to see the real address before clicking.
Never give a password or code in reply to a message.
Report scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk and texts to 7726.

check.q: Which of these is the **most** reliable sign that an email is phishing?
o: It asks you to type your password into a linked page
It was sent in the morning
check.why: Genuine companies never ask for your password via a link in an email.

check.q: What should you do to see where a link really goes?
o: Hover over it (or press and hold) to see the real address
check.why: Hovering reveals the true web address.

check.q: In `https://login.steam.com.free-skins.net/offer`, what is the real website?
check.why: The real domain is the part just before the first single slash: free-skins.net.

check.q: Where can you forward a scam text message in the UK?
check.why: 7726 is the free scam text reporting number.

practice.q: Give **three** features of an email that might suggest it is a phishing attempt.
practice.a: Any three: suspicious/misspelled sender address (1); urgent tone or threats (1); generic greeting e.g. Dear Customer (1); spelling/grammar errors (1); link to a strange web address (1); asks for password/personal/bank details (1); unexpected attachment (1); offer too good to be true (1).

practice.q: Aoife receives an email saying her school account will be locked unless she logs in using the link. Describe what she should do.
practice.a: Do not click the link / do not enter details (1); check another way, e.g. go to the school login page directly or ask a teacher (1); report it to a teacher / IT team (1); delete the email (1). Max 3.

practice.q: Explain why the advice is to go to a website yourself rather than clicking a link in a message.
practice.a: The link could lead to a fake website that copies the real one (1) and captures your login details / installs malware (1).

pages.spec: Explain what makes a password strong and how passphrases and password managers help
pages.summary: Length matters most. Long passphrases made of three random words are hard to crack but easy to remember, and a password manager lets you have a different strong password for every account.

diagram.title: How many possible passwords?
diagram.caption: Change the number of possible characters (10 = digits only, 26 = lowercase letters, 62 = upper, lower and digits, 94 = all keyboard characters) and the length, and watch the number of combinations grow.

blocks.text: Passwords are the front door key to your accounts. Criminals don't usually guess them one at a time by hand: they use software that can try **billions of guesses a second**. This is called a **[[Brute force attack]]**. They also try lists of the most common passwords first, like `123456`, `password` and `qwerty`.
Why length beats complexity
Each extra character **multiplies** the number of possible passwords. Try the calculator above: going from 8 to 12 characters makes a much bigger difference than adding a symbol.

blocks.title: Worked example: how long to try every password?
blocks.context: Imagine a computer that can try **10 billion** (10,000,000,000) passwords a second. How long would it take to try every possible password?
steps: 4-digit PIN: 10⁴ = 10,000 combinations, so less than a millisecond.
8 lowercase letters: 26⁸ ≈ 209 billion, so about **21 seconds**.
8 characters using upper, lower and digits: 62⁸ ≈ 218 trillion, so about **6 hours**.
20 lowercase letters (e.g. three random words): 26²⁰ is so big it would take about **63 billion years**.
blocks.answer: Length wins. A long passphrase of lowercase words is far stronger than a short, complicated password.

blocks.text: Use a passphrase

A **[[Passphrase]]** is a password made of several words. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends using **three random words**, such as `CactusTrumpetHarbour`. It is long, so it is hard to crack, but it is easy to picture and remember.

head: Weak
Why it is weak
Better
rows: A football team plus a number: in every hacker's word list.
Your name and birth year can be found on social media.
Swapping letters for symbols is a trick the software already knows.
blocks.caption: Making passwords stronger

blocks.text: One password per account
If you use the same password everywhere and **one** website is hacked, criminals will try that email and password on every other site. This is why every account needs a **different** password.

A **[[Password manager]]** is an app (or part of your browser) that creates and stores a different strong password for every account. You only need to remember **one** strong master password, which unlocks the rest.
Your **email** password is the most important of all, because it can be used to reset every other password. Make it long and unique, and protect it with two-factor authentication.
Never share your password, even with a best friend. Friendships change, and anything done from your account will look like it was done by **you**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Attackers use software to try billions of guesses: a brute force attack.
Length matters more than complexity.
Three random words make a strong, memorable passphrase.
Use a different password for every account.
A password manager stores them all behind one master password.

check.q: Which password is strongest?
check.why: It is the longest and made of random words.

check.q: What is a brute force attack?
o: Software trying every possible password until one works
check.why: It tries combinations very quickly until it finds the right one.

check.q: Why should you use a different password for each account?
o: If one site is hacked, your other accounts stay safe
check.why: Criminals try stolen passwords on other sites.

check.q: What does a password manager do?
o: Creates and stores strong passwords, unlocked by one master password
check.why: You only remember the master password.

practice.q: Explain why `CactusTrumpetHarbour` is a stronger password than `C@t5!`.
practice.a: It is much longer (1), so there are far more possible combinations / it would take much longer to brute force (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** benefits of using a password manager.
practice.a: Any two: you only need to remember one master password (1); it can generate long, strong random passwords (1); it allows a different password for every account (1); it can autofill so you avoid typing on fake sites (1).

practice.q: Give **three** pieces of advice for creating a secure password.
practice.a: Any three: make it long, e.g. 12+ characters (1); use three random words / a passphrase (1); do not use personal information like names, pets or birthdays (1); avoid common passwords/words (1); use a different password for each account (1); never share it (1).

pages.spec: Explain how two-factor and multi-factor authentication protect accounts
pages.summary: Authentication proves you are who you say you are. Two-factor authentication (2FA) asks for a second proof, such as a code on your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

diagram.title: Password only vs password + 2FA
diagram.caption: A criminal has stolen your password. What happens next?

states.label: Password only
points: The criminal types in your username and password
The website lets them straight in
They can read messages, change your password and lock you out
You may not find out until it is too late

states.label: Password + 2FA
points: The criminal types in your username and password
The website asks for a code from your phone
They do not have your phone, so they are stuck
You get an alert and can change your password

blocks.text: **[[Authentication]]** means proving you are who you say you are. When you type your username and password, the system checks they match before letting you in. But if someone has stolen your password, the system cannot tell them apart from you.
The three types of factor

head: Factor
Meaning
Examples
rows: A secret only you should know.
An object only you should have.
Your phone, a code-generating app, a security key, a bank card
blocks.caption: Authentication factors

blocks.text: **[[Two-factor authentication]]** (2FA) uses **two different types** of factor, for example a password (something you know) and a code sent to your phone (something you have). **[[Multi-factor authentication]]** (MFA) is the general name for using two or more factors.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it really 2FA?
blocks.context: Which of these logins use two-factor authentication?
steps: **Password + PIN:** both are *something you know*, so this is **not** true 2FA.
**Password + code from an authenticator app:** know + have, so **yes**.
**Bank card + PIN at a cash machine:** have + know, so **yes**.
**Phone unlocked with your face, then a banking app password:** are + know, so **yes**.
blocks.answer: 2FA needs two *different types* of factor, not just two things.

blocks.text: Common ways to get the second factor

items: **Text message (SMS) code:** easy to set up, but the weakest option because texts can sometimes be redirected.
**Authenticator app:** an app on your phone that shows a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds.
**Push notification:** your phone asks "Is this you trying to sign in?" and you tap Yes or No.
**Security key or passkey:** a physical key or your device's fingerprint/face unlock that proves it is you.

blocks.text: **Never share a 2FA code**, with anyone, ever. A common scam is a message or call saying "I sent you a code by mistake, can you send it to me?" They are trying to log in to **your** account.
If your phone asks you to approve a sign-in that you did not start, tap **No** (or Deny) and change your password. Someone else knows it.
Turn on 2FA for your email, games console account, and social media first. Most popular services have it in the **Security** or **Privacy** settings.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Authentication means proving who you are.
Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are.
2FA uses two different types of factor; MFA is two or more.
A stolen password alone is not enough to get past 2FA.
Never share a 2FA code with anyone.

check.q: Which pair is **true** two-factor authentication?
o: Password and a code from an authenticator app
check.why: Something you know + something you have.

check.q: A fingerprint is an example of:
check.why: Biometrics are 'something you are'.

check.q: A stranger messages you: "Oops, I sent my login code to your number, please send it back." What should you do?
o: Never share it: they are trying to get into your account
Reply asking who they are, then send it
check.why: This is a classic account takeover scam.

check.q: What does MFA stand for?
check.why: Two or more factors.

practice.q: Name the **three** types of authentication factor and give an example of each.
practice.a: Something you know, e.g. password/PIN (1); something you have, e.g. phone/security key/bank card (1); something you are, e.g. fingerprint/face (1).

practice.q: Explain how two-factor authentication protects an account if the password has been stolen.
practice.a: The attacker also needs the second factor, e.g. a code from the owner's phone (1), which they do not have, so they cannot log in (1).

practice.q: Explain why a password and a PIN together is **not** two-factor authentication.
practice.a: Both are 'something you know' (1); 2FA needs two different types of factor (1).

pages.spec: Explain what encryption is, use a Caesar cipher, and explain why the HTTPS padlock matters
pages.summary: Encryption scrambles data with a key so only someone with the right key can read it. The Caesar cipher is a simple historical example; HTTPS uses far stronger encryption to protect data sent to websites.

diagram.title: Encrypting a message
diagram.caption: Click each stage to follow the message from sender to receiver.

nodes.label: Plaintext
nodes.detail: The readable message: MEET AT LUNCH

nodes.label: Encrypt with key
nodes.detail: Each letter is shifted 3 places forward in the alphabet.

nodes.label: Ciphertext sent
nodes.detail: PHHW DW OXQFK: anyone who intercepts it just sees nonsense.

nodes.label: Decrypt with key
nodes.detail: The receiver shifts each letter 3 places back.

nodes.label: Plaintext again
nodes.detail: MEET AT LUNCH

blocks.text: When you send a message or log in to a website, your data travels through many other computers on the way. **[[Encryption]]** scrambles the data so that, even if someone intercepts it, they cannot read it. **[[Decryption]]** turns it back into readable data.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The secret information used to encrypt and decrypt, such as 'shift by 3'.
The method used to encrypt the message.
blocks.caption: Encryption vocabulary

blocks.text: The Caesar cipher

The **[[Caesar cipher]]** is named after Julius Caesar, who used it over 2,000 years ago to send secret military messages. Each letter is **shifted** a fixed number of places along the alphabet. The number of places is the **key**.

blocks.title: Worked example: encrypt MEET AT LUNCH with a key of 3
blocks.context: Shift every letter 3 places forward. After Z, wrap round to the start (X→A, Y→B, Z→C).
steps: Write the alphabet with the shifted alphabet underneath: A→D, B→E, C→F ... W→Z, X→A, Y→B, Z→C.
MEET: M→P, E→H, E→H, T→W gives **PHHW**.
AT: A→D, T→W gives **DW**.
LUNCH: L→O, U→X, N→Q, C→F, H→K gives **OXQFK**.
To decrypt, the receiver shifts each letter **back** 3 places.
blocks.answer: MEET AT LUNCH becomes PHHW DW OXQFK.

blocks.title: Caesar.cs: a Caesar cipher in C#

blocks.text: The Caesar cipher is **not secure**. There are only 25 possible keys, so anyone can try them all in a few minutes. Modern encryption uses keys so long that trying every one would take longer than the age of the universe.
HTTPS and the padlock

**[[HTTPS]]** (HyperText Transfer Protocol **Secure**) is the encrypted version of HTTP, the rules for sending web pages. When a site uses HTTPS, your browser shows a **padlock** or similar icon, and the address starts with `https://`.

head: HTTP
HTTPS
rows: Yes: encrypted between your browser and the website
Could someone on the same Wi-Fi read it?
Safe for logging in or paying?
Yes, as long as the website itself is genuine

blocks.text: The padlock means the connection is **encrypted**, not that the website is **honest**. Many phishing sites have a padlock too. Always check the web address as well.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Encryption scrambles plaintext into ciphertext using a key.
Only someone with the key can decrypt it.
The Caesar cipher shifts each letter a fixed number of places.
Caesar is easy to crack: there are only 25 keys.
HTTPS encrypts data sent to websites; the padlock does not prove the site is genuine.

check.q: Using a Caesar cipher with a key of 3, what does CAT become?
check.why: C→F, A→D, T→W.

check.q: What is ciphertext?
check.why: Ciphertext is what an interceptor would see.

check.q: Why is the Caesar cipher easy to crack?
o: There are only 25 possible keys to try
check.why: You can try every shift quickly.

check.q: What does the padlock next to a web address tell you?
o: The connection between you and the site is encrypted
The site is run by the government
check.why: It shows HTTPS encryption, not honesty.

practice.q: Encrypt the word `HELLO` using a Caesar cipher with a key of 3. Show your working.
practice.a: Working showing each letter shifted 3 places, e.g. H→K, E→H, L→O (1); answer KHOOR (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **encryption** and why it is used.
practice.a: Scrambling data/converting plaintext to ciphertext using a key (1) so that if it is intercepted it cannot be understood without the key (1).

practice.q: A pupil says: "The site has a padlock, so it must be safe to enter my password." Explain why the pupil may be wrong.
practice.a: The padlock only shows the connection is encrypted/HTTPS (1); a fake/phishing website can also have a padlock, so you must check the web address too (1).

pages.spec: Describe how firewalls, anti-malware, updates and backups protect computer systems
pages.summary: No single defence stops everything, so systems use layers: firewalls control network traffic, anti-malware finds harmful software, updates patch security holes, and backups let you recover.

diagram.title: Layers of defence
diagram.caption: Like a castle with walls, a moat and guards, good security has several layers. If one fails, the next can still stop the attack. Click each layer.

items.label: You: careful, aware users
items.detail: Spotting phishing, not sharing passwords and reporting problems stops many attacks before they start.

items.label: Strong passwords and 2FA
items.detail: Stop criminals getting into accounts even if they try.

items.label: Anti-malware software
items.detail: Scans files and blocks known malware.

items.label: Updates and patches
items.detail: Fix the security holes that malware such as worms tries to use.

items.label: Firewall
items.detail: Checks network traffic coming in and going out and blocks anything not allowed.

items.label: Backups
items.detail: The last line of defence: if everything else fails, you can restore your data.

blocks.text: Organisations like schools, banks and hospitals use several layers of protection at the same time. This is sometimes called **defence in depth**. You can use the same ideas at home.
Firewalls

A **[[Firewall]]** sits between a computer (or a whole network) and the internet. It checks the data travelling in and out against a set of **rules** and blocks anything that is not allowed, a bit like a security guard checking passes at the school gate.

items: A firewall can be **software** (built into Windows and macOS) or **hardware** (a separate box, or part of your home router).
It can block unknown programs from sending data out of your computer.
It can stop outside computers connecting to your computer without permission.
It does **not** stop you choosing to download malware or type your password into a phishing site.

blocks.text: Anti-malware software

**[[Anti-malware software]]** (often still called antivirus) scans files, downloads and emails for malware. It compares them against a huge list of known malware **signatures** and watches for suspicious **behaviour**, such as a program suddenly encrypting hundreds of files. Infected files are **quarantined** (locked away) or deleted.
Anti-malware can only recognise new threats if it is **kept up to date**. Most programs update themselves automatically, so don't turn this off.
Updates and patches

Software often contains mistakes that attackers can use to get in. When the company finds one, it releases a **[[Patch]]**: an update that fixes the hole. Installing updates promptly is one of the most effective things anyone can do. Remember WannaCry: it only infected computers that had not installed a patch released two months earlier.
Backups
A **[[Backup]]** is a separate copy of your data. If files are deleted, corrupted, stolen or locked by ransomware, you can restore them from the backup. A popular rule is **3-2-1**:

items: **3** copies of your important data,
on **2** different types of storage (e.g. laptop and external drive),
with **1** copy kept somewhere else (e.g. in the cloud or at a different building).

blocks.title: Worked example: protecting a family computer
blocks.context: The Murphy family's laptop is used for homework, photos and online banking. What layers of protection should they use?
steps: Turn on the built-in **firewall** and the router's firewall.
Keep the built-in **anti-malware** switched on and updating.
Set **automatic updates** for the operating system, browser and apps.
Back up photos and homework to the **cloud** and an **external drive** (3-2-1).
Give each person their own account with a strong passphrase and **2FA** on email and banking.
blocks.answer: Several layers together, so that if one fails another still protects them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Defence in depth means using several layers of protection.
A firewall filters network traffic using rules.
Anti-malware scans for and quarantines harmful software.
Patches fix security holes, so install updates promptly.
Backups (3-2-1 rule) let you recover from ransomware, accidents and hardware failure.

check.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Checks and filters network traffic using rules
check.why: It controls what data can come in and go out.

check.q: Why should you install software updates promptly?
o: They often patch security holes attackers could use
check.why: Unpatched holes are how worms like WannaCry spread.

check.q: In the 3-2-1 backup rule, what does the '1' stand for?
check.why: Keeping one copy elsewhere protects against fire, theft and ransomware.

check.q: What happens to a file when anti-malware quarantines it?
o: It is emailed to your friends
It is locked away so it cannot run
It is encrypted with a Caesar cipher
check.why: Quarantine isolates the suspicious file.

practice.q: Describe how a firewall helps protect a school network.
practice.a: It checks/monitors data coming into and leaving the network (1) and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules / unauthorised access (1).

practice.q: Explain why keeping backups is a good defence against ransomware.
practice.a: The organisation can restore its files from the backup (1) so it does not need to pay the ransom / loses little data (1).

practice.q: Give **three** different methods a home user could use to protect their computer from malware and explain each briefly.
practice.a: Any three with brief explanation: anti-malware software scans and removes malware (1); firewall blocks unauthorised network traffic (1); install updates/patches to fix security holes (1); avoid suspicious links/downloads (1); regular backups to recover files (1).

pages.spec: Describe, in simple terms, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and data protection law (UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018)
pages.summary: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a crime to access or damage computers without permission. UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 set rules for how organisations must collect, use and protect personal data.

diagram.title: Is it against the Computer Misuse Act?
diagram.caption: Decide whether each action breaks the law, then click to check.
head: Action
Illegal?
Why
rows: Logging into a friend's game account with their password, without asking
Unauthorised access: knowing the password is not the same as having permission
Reading a teacher's files on a computer they forgot to lock
Logging into your own school account
You are authorised to use it
Writing and spreading a virus 'as a joke'
Deliberately impairing computers is a serious offence
A company paying an ethical hacker to test its own website
The owner has given written permission
Guessing a classmate's password to change their profile picture

blocks.text: Laws help protect computer systems and personal data. In the UK there are two main laws you need to know about for cyber security.
The Computer Misuse Act 1990

The **[[Computer Misuse Act 1990]]** was passed after two people hacked into a British Telecom system in the 1980s and could not be properly charged, because no law covered hacking at the time. The Act makes the following illegal:

head: Offence
In simple terms
Example
rows: Getting into a computer, account or files you do not have permission to use.
Logging in as a friend using a password you saw them type.
Unauthorised access with intent to commit or help with further crimes
Getting in, **in order to** commit another crime.
Accessing someone's account in order to steal money from them.
Unauthorised acts that impair a computer
Deliberately damaging, deleting or stopping a computer or data from working.
Spreading malware, or flooding a website so it crashes.
Making, supplying or obtaining tools for computer misuse
Creating or handing out programs meant to be used for these crimes.
blocks.caption: Offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (as updated)

blocks.text: The Act has been updated since 1990 (for example in 2006 and 2015) to cover newer threats. Penalties range from fines to long prison sentences for the most serious offences.
"I was only messing about" is not a defence. Using someone else's login without permission, even as a joke and even if they told you their password ages ago, can break the Computer Misuse Act.
Data protection: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018

**[[Personal data]]** is any information that can identify a living person: your name, address, photo, email, date of birth, and so on. Organisations that hold personal data, like your school, doctor or a games company, must follow the **[[UK GDPR]]** (UK General Data Protection Regulation) and the **[[Data Protection Act 2018]]**. Together they set the rules for how personal data must be handled.

head: Principle (simplified)
What it means
rows: Be honest about what data you collect and why.
Only use it for the reason you collected it.
Only collect what you actually need.
Keep it correct and up to date.
Don't keep it for longer than needed.
Keep it safe from loss, theft and hackers.
Be able to show that you follow the rules.
blocks.caption: The data protection principles

blocks.text: You also have **rights** over your data. For example, you can ask an organisation for a copy of the data it holds about you (a *subject access request*), ask for mistakes to be corrected, and in some cases ask for it to be deleted. The law is enforced by the **Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)**, which can fine organisations that break the rules, sometimes by millions of pounds.

blocks.title: Worked example: a school data breach
blocks.context: A teacher leaves an unencrypted memory stick containing pupils' names, addresses and medical notes on a bus. Which principle has been broken, and what should the school do?
steps: The data was not kept secure: the **integrity and confidentiality (security)** principle has been broken.
The school must assess the risk and, if it is serious, report the breach to the **ICO** (normally within 72 hours).
It may need to tell the families affected.
To stop it happening again: encrypt devices and use secure cloud storage instead of memory sticks.
blocks.answer: Data protection law means organisations must protect personal data, not just collect it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to computers illegal.
It also covers accessing computers to commit further crimes, and damaging or impairing them.
UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 control how personal data is used and protected.
Organisations must collect only what they need and keep it secure.
The ICO enforces data protection law in the UK.

check.q: Which law makes hacking into someone's account illegal?
o: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
check.why: Unauthorised access is the first offence under the Computer Misuse Act.

check.q: Which of these is **personal data**?
check.why: It can identify a living person.

check.q: Which organisation enforces data protection law in the UK?
check.why: The Information Commissioner's Office.

check.q: A club collects members' blood type when it only needs their name and email. Which principle is broken?
check.why: Only collect what you need.

practice.q: Describe **two** offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
practice.a: Any two: unauthorised access to computer material (1); unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (1); unauthorised acts that impair/damage a computer or data, e.g. spreading malware (1); making/supplying tools for computer misuse (1).

practice.q: Give **three** rules (principles) that organisations must follow under UK GDPR / the Data Protection Act 2018.
practice.a: Any three: processed lawfully, fairly and transparently (1); used only for the stated purpose (1); only collect data that is needed (1); kept accurate and up to date (1); not kept longer than necessary (1); kept secure (1); organisation is accountable (1).

practice.q: Sam uses a password he saw his friend type to log in to her social media account and post a message. Explain whether Sam has broken the law.
practice.a: Yes, under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (1) because he accessed the account without permission / unauthorised access, even though he knew the password (1).

pages.spec: Explain what ethical hacking is and describe careers and competitions in cyber security
pages.summary: Ethical hackers are paid, with permission, to find weaknesses before criminals do. Cyber security is a fast-growing career, and competitions like CyberFirst let you try it while still at school.

diagram.title: A pathway into cyber security
diagram.caption: One possible route from KS3 to a cyber career. There are many others!

items.label: Years 8 to 10: KS3
items.detail: Learn the basics, try coding, enter competitions such as the CyberFirst Girls Competition.

items.label: Years 11 to 12: GCSE
items.detail: GCSE Digital Technology (or Computer Science) builds programming and networking skills.

items.label: Years 13 to 14: A level or BTEC
items.detail: Software Systems Development, Digital Technology, maths or physics; CyberFirst courses in the holidays.

items.label: University or apprenticeship
items.detail: A cyber security or computing degree, or a degree apprenticeship where you earn while you learn.

items.label: First job
items.detail: Security analyst, penetration tester, digital forensics, security engineer...

blocks.text: Not all hackers are criminals. Organisations **pay** skilled people to try to break into their own systems, so that weaknesses can be fixed before a real attacker finds them. This is called **[[Ethical hacking]]**.

head: Ethical (white hat) hacker
Criminal (black hat) hacker
rows: Yes: written permission from the owner
What happens to what they find?
Reported privately to the owner so it can be fixed
No: breaks the Computer Misuse Act 1990

blocks.text: A **[[Penetration testing]]** job (a 'pen test') is a planned, agreed test where an ethical hacker attacks a system within agreed rules and then writes a report explaining what they found and how to fix it. Some companies also run *bug bounty* programmes, paying rewards to people who report security flaws responsibly.

Permission is everything. Testing a website, a school network or a friend's account **without** written permission is a crime, even if you mean well. Practise only on legal training sites and competitions designed for it.
Careers in cyber security

head: Job
What they do
rows: Watches an organisation's systems for signs of attack and responds when something happens.
Tests systems, with permission, to find weaknesses before criminals do.
Examines computers and phones after a crime to find evidence, often working with the police.
Designs and builds secure networks and software.
Teaches staff how to spot phishing and keep data safe.
blocks.caption: Some cyber security jobs

blocks.text: There are not enough trained people to fill all the cyber security jobs, so skills are in high demand. Northern Ireland, and Belfast in particular, has a large and growing cyber security industry with many international companies.
Competitions and programmes

items: **[[CyberFirst]]** is run by the **National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)**, part of GCHQ. It includes the **CyberFirst Girls Competition** for teams of girls (in Northern Ireland it is aimed at Year 9), free courses for young people, and bursaries for university students.
**Capture the Flag (CTF)** competitions give you safe, legal puzzles to solve, such as cracking a cipher or finding a hidden clue in a file.
Many universities and companies run cyber summer schools and work experience for school pupils.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it ethical hacking?
blocks.context: Decide whether each person is acting ethically and legally.
steps: **Niamh** is hired by a bank, signs an agreement, tests its app and reports a flaw: **ethical and legal**.
**Jack** finds a way to see other pupils' files on the school network and tries it 'to see if it works': **not ethical, not legal**. He should have told IT staff without testing it.
**Priya** solves cipher puzzles in a CyberFirst competition: **ethical and legal**, it is designed for that.
**Tom** guesses a gaming site's admin password to prove it is weak, then emails them: **illegal**, because he had no permission first.
blocks.answer: Ethical hacking always starts with permission and ends with a private report.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Ethical hackers test systems with permission so weaknesses can be fixed.
Penetration testing is an agreed, planned attack followed by a report.
Without permission it is a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
Cyber security skills are in high demand, including in Northern Ireland.
CyberFirst (run by the NCSC) offers competitions, courses and bursaries.

check.q: What is the main difference between an ethical hacker and a criminal hacker?
o: Ethical hackers have permission from the system owner
Criminal hackers only work at night
check.why: Permission makes it legal.

check.q: What is penetration testing?
o: Testing how strong a screen is
An agreed, planned attack on a system to find weaknesses
check.why: It is followed by a report to fix the weaknesses.

check.q: Who runs CyberFirst?
check.why: The NCSC is part of GCHQ.

check.q: A pupil discovers a way to see other pupils' files on the school network. What should they do?
o: Look at the files to check
Report it privately to a teacher or IT staff without testing it
check.why: Reporting responsibly, without accessing data, is the right thing to do.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **ethical hacking**.
practice.a: Legally attempting to break into/find weaknesses in a system (1) with the owner's permission so they can be fixed (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** jobs in cyber security.
practice.a: Any two with description: security analyst monitors systems for attacks (1); penetration tester tests systems for weaknesses with permission (1); digital forensics investigator finds evidence on devices (1); security engineer designs secure systems (1); awareness trainer teaches staff (1).

practice.q: Explain why it is illegal for a pupil to test the school network for weaknesses even if they intend to report what they find.
practice.a: They do not have permission/authorisation from the owner (1), so it is unauthorised access under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (1).

chapters.title: Databases
chapters.intro: Databases run your school, your supermarket and your GP surgery. Learn how to design a table in Microsoft Access, keep the data accurate with validation and verification, and find exactly what you need with queries, forms and reports.

pages.spec: Explain what a database is, give examples of where databases are used and describe the difference between data and information
pages.summary: A database is an organised collection of related data that can be searched, sorted and updated quickly. Databases are everywhere: in school, in shops, in libraries and in hospitals. Data is raw facts; information is data with meaning.

diagram.title: Who uses this data?
diagram.caption: Click to match each organisation with what its database is used for.
pairs: Reordering products when stock runs low
Checking a patient's allergies before prescribing
Chasing members who have not paid their fees

blocks.text: Every time you are marked present at registration, scan a library book or buy something with a loyalty card, data is being saved in a **[[database]]**. A database is an **organised collection of related data**, stored so that it can be found, sorted and changed quickly.

In this topic you will use **Microsoft Access**, a **[[database management system (DBMS)|Database management system]]**. A DBMS is the software that lets you build the database, enter data, search it and print results.
Where are databases used?

head: Organisation
What the database stores
What it is used for
rows: Pupil names, addresses, tutor groups, attendance, timetables, behaviour points, exam results
The school's **[[MIS|Management information system]]** (for example SIMS, used in many schools) prints registers, reports and timetables and lets staff contact parents
Products, prices, stock levels, loyalty card customers
Updating stock at the till, reordering when stock is low, sending money-off vouchers
Books, members, loans and return dates
Finding a book, checking who has it, sending overdue reminders
Hospital or GP surgery (Health and Social Care in NI)
Patients, appointments, medicines, allergies, test results
Any doctor can quickly see a patient's history and allergies
Picking teams, chasing unpaid fees, contacting players
blocks.caption: Some everyday databases

blocks.text: Why not just use paper?

head: Paper records (filing cabinet)
Electronic database
rows: Slow: someone has to look through every card
Very fast: a query searches thousands of records in a second
One click sorts A to Z or by date
Crossing out and rewriting gets messy
Change the data once and it is updated everywhere
Stored on a server or in the cloud
Anyone with the key can read it; fire or flood destroys it
Passwords and access levels; backups can be kept

blocks.text: Data or information?
**[[Data]]** is raw facts and figures with no meaning on their own. **[[Information]]** is data that has been processed and given **context**, so it means something.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning data into information
blocks.context: You find this on a scrap of paper: `BT74 7HN   14   87`
steps: On its own it is just **data**: a postcode, a number and another number. We do not know what they mean.
Add context: *Pupil's postcode*, *Age*, *Maths test score (%)*.
Now it becomes **information**: a 14-year-old pupil living in BT74 7HN scored 87% in a Maths test.
blocks.answer: Data + context (meaning) = information.

blocks.text: Because databases hold personal data, organisations must follow the **Data Protection Act 2018** (UK GDPR). Data must be kept secure, accurate and only used for the reason it was collected.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A database is an organised collection of related data.
A DBMS such as Microsoft Access is used to create and search a database.
Schools, shops, libraries and hospitals all rely on databases.
Databases are faster to search, sort and update than paper records.
Data = raw facts; information = data with context and meaning.

check.q: What is a database?
o: An organised collection of related data
check.why: A database stores related data in an organised way so it can be searched and sorted.

check.q: Which of these is **information** rather than data?
check.why: It has context: we know what the data means.

check.q: Which software is a database management system?
check.why: Access is used to create and manage databases.

check.q: Which is an advantage of an electronic database over paper records?
o: It can be searched far more quickly
check.why: Queries search thousands of records in seconds. Electronic data can still be wrong or hacked.

practice.q: State **two** places that use a database and, for each, give one item of data it would store.
practice.a: Any two places (1 each), each with a suitable data item (1 each), e.g. school (1) stores pupils' attendance (1); library (1) stores loan return dates (1); supermarket (1) stores stock levels (1); hospital/GP (1) stores patient allergies (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between data and information, using an example.
practice.a: Data is raw facts/figures with no meaning (1). Information is data that has been processed/given context so it has meaning (1). Suitable example, e.g. '15' is data; 'Sam is 15 years old' is information (1).

practice.q: Give **two** advantages of a library storing its records in a database instead of on paper cards.
practice.a: Any two (1 each): faster to search for a book; easy to sort; easy to update/change details; takes up less space; can be backed up; can be password protected; overdue reminders can be produced automatically.

pages.spec: Identify tables, records and fields in a database
pages.summary: Data in Access is stored in tables. Each row is a record (one person or thing) and each column is a field (one item of data about every record).

diagram.title: Field, record or table?
diagram.caption: Decide which each item is, then click to check.
head: Item
Answer
Why
rows: One item of data stored about every pupil
All the data about one pupil
The whole collection of pupil records
All the data about one library book
One row in the Books table
Stores records about one type of thing

blocks.text: A database is made of one or more **[[tables|Table]]**. Each table stores data about **one type of thing**: pupils, books, products or patients. A small database might have only one table; a school MIS has hundreds.

head: PupilID
FirstName
Surname
TutorGroup
DateOfBirth
Town
blocks.caption: The Pupils table, shown in Datasheet view

blocks.text: Records and fields

items: A **[[record]]** is **one row**: all the data about one pupil. The table above has **4 records**.
A **[[field]]** is **one column**: one item of data stored about every pupil. The table above has **6 fields**.
The **[[field name]]** is the heading at the top of each column, e.g. `Surname`.
Each **cell** holds one item of data, e.g. *Lisnaskea* is the Town for record 1002.

blocks.text: Remember: **R**ecord = **R**ow (going across). **F**ield = the column that goes **f**rom top to bottom.
Naming fields
Good field names are **short, clear and meaningful**. Avoid spaces and odd symbols: they can cause problems later in queries. Many people write names in *CamelCase*, e.g. `DateOfBirth`, `TutorGroup`.

head: Good field name
Poor field name
rows: `the date that the pupil was born` (far too long)

blocks.text: Views in Access

Access shows a table in two main ways. **[[Datasheet view]]** shows the data in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet; you use it to type in and look at records. **Design view** shows the structure of the table (the field names and their data types). You will use Design view on page 4.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting records and fields
blocks.context: A sports club table has the field names MemberID, FirstName, Surname, Team and FeesPaid. There are 38 members.
steps: Each member is one row, so there are **38 records**.
Each field name is one column, so there are **5 fields**.
The data about *all* members is held in **one table**, e.g. *Members*.
blocks.answer: 38 records, 5 fields, 1 table.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A table stores data about one type of thing.
A record is one row: everything about one person or thing.
A field is one column: one item of data about every record.
Field names should be short, clear and have no spaces.
Datasheet view shows the data; Design view shows the structure.

check.q: In a table of pupils, what is a **record**?
o: All the data about one pupil
check.why: A record is a row: all the data about one person or thing.

check.q: In the Pupils table on this page, how many **fields** are there?
check.why: PupilID, FirstName, Surname, TutorGroup, DateOfBirth, Town.

check.q: Which is the best field name for a pupil's home phone number?
check.why: Short, meaningful and no spaces or symbols.

check.q: Which view in Access shows the data in rows and columns like a spreadsheet?
check.why: Datasheet view shows the records.

practice.q: Using the Pupils table on this page, identify **one** record and **one** field.
practice.a: Record: any one full row, e.g. 1003, Niamh, Maguire, 9A, 02/06/2012, Enniskillen (1). Field: any one column/field name, e.g. Town (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a record and a field.
practice.a: A record is all the data about one person/thing / one row (1). A field is one item/category of data stored about each record / one column (1).

practice.q: A library stores details of its books. Suggest **three** suitable field names for its Books table.
practice.a: Any three sensible, well-formed names (1 each), e.g. BookID, Title, Author, ISBN, Genre, DatePublished, OnLoan.

pages.spec: Choose a suitable data type for each field in a table
pages.summary: Every field has a data type that controls what can be stored in it. Choosing the right data type stops wrong data being entered and lets Access sort and calculate correctly.

diagram.title: Pick the data type
diagram.caption: Choose a data type for each field, then click to check.
head: Field
Data type
Reason
rows: May be added up for a season total

blocks.text: When you create a field in Access you must choose its **[[data type]]**. This tells Access what *kind* of data the field will hold. Getting it right means Access can stop silly mistakes (like typing *abc* into an age field), sort the data properly and do calculations.

head: Access data type
What it stores
Example fields
rows: Letters, numbers and symbols, up to 255 characters
Large amounts of text (more than 255 characters)
Numbers you might do calculations with
Money values, shown with a £ sign and 2 decimal places
A unique number Access adds automatically for each new record
Only two possible values: Yes/No, True/False, On/Off
blocks.caption: The main data types in Microsoft Access

blocks.text: **Phone numbers are Short Text, not Number!** A Number field would remove the leading zero, so `02866 322 112` would become `2866322112`, and the spaces would not be allowed. You never do maths with a phone number, so store it as text. The same goes for postcodes and house numbers like *12A*.
A quick test: *Would I ever add, subtract or average this?* If not, it probably should not be a Number field.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing data types for a tuck shop table
blocks.context: The school tuck shop wants a Products table with the fields ProductID, ProductName, Price, StockLevel, DateLastOrdered and Vegetarian.
steps: **ProductID**: AutoNumber, so every product automatically gets its own unique number.
**ProductName**: Short Text, e.g. *Tayto Cheese and Onion*.
**Price**: Currency, e.g. £0.80.
**StockLevel**: Number, because we subtract each time one is sold.
**DateLastOrdered**: Date/Time, so Access can sort the dates in order.
**Vegetarian**: Yes/No, because the answer can only be yes or no.
blocks.answer: AutoNumber, Short Text, Currency, Number, Date/Time, Yes/No.

blocks.text: Why does the data type matter?

items: It acts as a **type check**: Access rejects data of the wrong type (you cannot enter *twelve* into a Number field).
Dates stored as Date/Time **sort correctly** (by year, month, day) instead of alphabetically.
Number and Currency fields can be used in **calculations** such as totals and averages.
A Yes/No field shows as a simple **tick box**, which is quick to fill in.

blocks.text: In your GCSE course you may see these described with general names: *text/string*, *integer*, *real/float*, *date*, *Boolean*. Access's Number field can hold whole numbers (integers) or decimals (real numbers).

blocks.title: Key points
items: Every field must have a data type.
Main Access types: Short Text, Long Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, AutoNumber, Yes/No.
Phone numbers and postcodes are Short Text.
Use Currency for money and Yes/No for two-option answers.
The right data type stops wrong data and allows correct sorting and calculations.

check.q: Which data type should be used for a pupil's mobile number?
check.why: The leading zero must be kept and no calculations are done on it.

check.q: Which data type is best for the price of a school dinner?
check.why: Currency shows £ and two decimal places.

check.q: A field records whether a library book is currently on loan. Which data type is best?
check.why: There are only two possible values.

check.q: What does an AutoNumber field do?
o: Adds up all the numbers in a column
Gives each new record a unique number automatically
check.why: Access fills it in for you: 1, 2, 3...

practice.q: A dentist stores PatientID, Surname, DateOfLastVisit, AmountOwed and NeedsReminder. State the most suitable data type for **each** field.
practice.a: PatientID: AutoNumber (or Number/Short Text) (1). Surname: Short Text (1). DateOfLastVisit: Date/Time (1). AmountOwed: Currency (1). NeedsReminder: Yes/No (1).

practice.q: Explain why a phone number should be stored as Short Text and not as a Number.
practice.a: A Number field would remove the leading zero / cannot store spaces or + symbols (1). No calculations are ever done on a phone number (1).

practice.q: Give **one** reason why choosing the correct data type is important.
practice.a: Any one (1): stops data of the wrong type being entered / acts as a type check; allows correct sorting (e.g. dates); allows calculations; saves storage space.

pages.spec: Explain what a primary key is and design a table with suitable field names, data types and a primary key
pages.summary: A primary key is a field that is different for every record, so each record can be identified. A good table design lists every field with its name, data type, a description and any validation.

diagram.title: Creating a table in Access
diagram.caption: The steps to build a table from your design.

nodes.label: Create
nodes.detail: Create tab, then Table Design.
